summary.text: For \(n=550172=4\cdot343\cdot401\), periodicity and CRT reduce a finite modular computation showing that the residue \(13573\) is never attained for \(k\le 16331503\), so \(a(n)\ge 16331504\). A prime-counting sieve shows that the \(550172\)-nd prime is below \(8165754\), hence \(2(p_n-1)\le 16331504\), contradicting the proposed strict bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
f_n(k)\equiv 2^k-k\pmod n,
\]
and let \(a(n)\) be the least positive integer \(m\) for which the values \(f_n(1),\ldots,f_n(m)\) contain every residue modulo \(n\). We disprove the conjecture with
\[
N=550172.
\]
The factorization
\[
N=4\cdot137543=4\cdot343\cdot401=196\cdot2807
\]
will be used repeatedly. The residue that will obstruct early coverage is
\[
r_0=13573.
\]
We shall prove
\[
a(N)\ge 16331504.
\]
The \(550172\)-nd prime is \(8165753\), and hence
\[
2(p_{550172}-1)=2(8165753-1)=16331504.
\]
Thus this lower bound directly contradicts the conjectured strict inequality.

We first establish the modular facts used both to show that \(a(N)\) exists and to reduce the avoidance calculation to a manageable finite calculation.

## 1. A period modulo \(N\)

Direct repeated-squaring calculations give
\[
2^{147}\equiv1\pmod{343},\qquad 2^{200}\equiv1\pmod{401}.
\]
Since \(29400=147\cdot200\), it follows that
\[
2^{29400}\equiv1\pmod{343},\qquad
2^{29400}\equiv1\pmod{401}.
\]
The moduli \(343\) and \(401\) are coprime, so
\[
2^{29400}\equiv1\pmod{137543}.
\]
On the other hand, if \(a\ge2\), both \(2^a\) and \(2^{a+29400t}\) are divisible by \(4\). Combining the congruences modulo \(4\) and modulo \(137543\) gives, for every \(a\ge2\) and \(t\ge0\),
\[
2^{a+29400t}\equiv2^a\pmod N. \tag{1}
\]
Consequently,
\[
f_N(a+29400t)\equiv f_N(a)-29400t\pmod N. \tag{2}
\]

We shall also use
\[
29400=196\cdot150,
\qquad N=196\cdot2807,
\]
and the elementary inverse calculation
\[
150\cdot131=19650=7\cdot2807+1,
\]
so that
\[
150^{-1}\equiv131\pmod{2807}. \tag{3}
\]

## 2. An explicit construction showing that all residues are eventually hit

The following table has one entry for each residue \(s=0,1,\ldots,195\), in that order:
\[
\begin{split}
A={}&[36,143,2,349,308,3,26,225,332,191,50,81,4,31,58,85,48,139,98,193,\
&220,15,122,237,328,287,146,5,204,311,170,29,60,171,10,37,64,27,118,77,\
&172,199,226,101,216,307,266,125,72,183,290,149,8,39,150,173,16,43,6,97,\
&56,151,178,205,80,195,286,245,104,51,162,269,128,475,18,129,152,11,22,49,\
&76,35,130,157,184,59,174,265,224,83,30,141,248,107,454,413,108,131,330,437,\
&28,55,14,109,136,163,38,153,244,203,62,9,120,227,86,433,392,87,110,309,416,\
&7,34,61,88,115,142,17,132,223,182,41,304,99,206,65,412,371,66,89,288,395,\
&254,13,40,67,94,121,148,111,202,161,20,283,78,185,44,391,350,45,68,267,374,\
&233,12,19,46,73,100,127,90,181,140,235,262,57,164,23,370,329,24,47,246,353,\
&212,71,102,25,52,79,106,69,160,119,214,241].
\end{split}
\]
A finite modular calculation, performed by repeated doubling modulo \(196\), gives for every \(s\in\{0,\\ldots,195\}\), with \(a=A_s\),
\[
2\le a\le475,
\qquad 2^a-a\equiv s\pmod{196}. \tag{4}
\]
This table is not asserting a large exponentiation in the integers: starting with \(1\), one repeatedly doubles and reduces modulo \(196\), then subtracts \(a\). Thus (4) is a finite list of 196 small modular checks.

We now explain how this small table produces a hit modulo \(N\) for every residue. Fix \(r\), \(0\le r<N\), let \(s=r\bmod196\), and put \(a=A_s\). Let
\[
b=(2^a-a)\bmod N,
\]
where \(0\le b<N\). Since \(196\mid N\), equation (4) implies
\[
b\equiv r\pmod{196}. \tag{5}
\]
Define
\[
\delta=(b+N-r)\bmod N.
\]
By (5), \(196\mid\delta\). Write \(d=\delta/196\), and define
\[
t=(131d)\bmod2807,
\qquad k=a+29400t. \tag{6}
\]
By (3),
\[
150t\equiv d\pmod{2807}.
\]
Multiplying by \(196\) gives
\[
29400t\equiv\delta\pmod N. \tag{7}
\]
The definition of \(\delta\) says \(b\equiv r+\delta\pmod N\). Therefore (7) gives
\[
b-29400t\equiv r\pmod N.
\]
Using (2), we conclude
\[
2^k-k=f_N(k)\equiv r\pmod N. \tag{8}
\]
Moreover, \(a\le475\) and \(0\le t\le2806\), so
\[
1\le k\le475+29400\cdot2806=82496875. \tag{9}
\]
Thus every residue modulo \(N\) is hit by some positive \(k\le82496875\). In particular, the set of cutoff values giving complete coverage is nonempty, so its least member \(a(N)\) exists. This explicit existence argument is included because later we take a lower bound on that least member.

## 3. Reduction of the missing-residue assertion

We now prove that \(r_0=13573\) is not hit by any
\[
1\le k\le M,
\qquad M=16331503. \tag{10}
\]

The case \(k=1\) is immediate:
\[
2^1-1=1\not\equiv13573\pmod N,
\]
since both numbers lie between \(0\) and \(N-1\) and are unequal.

Suppose henceforth that \(k\ge2\). Divide \(k-2\) by \(29400\), and write
\[
a=(k-2)\bmod29400+2,
\qquad q=\left\lfloor\frac{k-2}{29400}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then
\[
2\le a\le29401,
\qquad k=a+29400q. \tag{11}
\]
By (1),
\[
2^k-k\equiv(2^a-a)-29400q\pmod N. \tag{12}
\]
For each \(a\) in the finite interval \(2\le a\le29401\), define
\[
b_a=(2^a-a)\bmod N.
\]
If (12) is congruent to \(r_0\), reduction modulo \(196\) gives the necessary condition
\[
b_a\equiv r_0\pmod{196}, \tag{13}
\]
because \(196\mid29400\). If (13) holds, set
\[
\delta_a=(b_a+N-r_0)\bmod N,
\quad d_a=\delta_a/196,
\quad t_a=(131d_a)\bmod2807,
\]
and define
\[
F(a)=a+29400t_a. \tag{14}
\]
Exactly as in (7), condition (13) implies
\[
29400t_a\equiv\delta_a\pmod N,
\]
so \(F(a)\) is a hit of \(r_0\).

More importantly, (14) identifies every possible hit below our cutoff. Indeed, suppose \(k=a+29400q\le M\) hits \(r_0\). Then
\[
b_a\equiv r_0+29400q\pmod N.
\]
After subtracting \(r_0\), dividing the resulting congruence by \(196\), and using \(29400/196=150\), we obtain
\[
150q\equiv d_a\pmod{2807}.
\]
Multiplication by the inverse \(131\) gives
\[
q\equiv t_a\pmod{2807}. \tag{15}
\]
The cutoff implies \(q<2807\), while by definition \(0\le t_a<2807\). Hence (15) forces \(q=t_a\), and therefore
\[
k=F(a). \tag{16}
\]
Thus it remains only to inspect the 29400 possible values of \(a\). For each one, either (13) fails, or its unique possible hit in the relevant congruence class is the explicitly computed number \(F(a)\).

Here is a fully explicit description of the finite modular calculation used for that inspection. It avoids ever forming \(2^a\) as a large integer. For each \(a=2,3,\ldots,29401\), calculate
\[
u=2^{a\bmod147}\bmod343,
\qquad v=2^{a\bmod200}\bmod401.
\]
Since \(401\cdot207\equiv1\pmod{343}\) and \(343\cdot159\equiv1\pmod{401}\), put
\[
y=(u\cdot401\cdot207+v\cdot343\cdot159)\bmod137543.
\]
The two period congruences at the beginning show that
\[
y\equiv2^a\pmod{137543}.
\]
Also
\[
4\cdot34386\equiv1\pmod{137543}.
\]
Because \(a\ge2\), \(2^a\equiv0\pmod4\). Therefore the simultaneous solution modulo \(4\cdot137543=N\) is
\[
P_a=4\bigl((34386y)\bmod137543\bigr)\bmod N,
\]
and \(P_a=2^a\bmod N\). Hence
\[
b_a=(P_a+N-(a\bmod N))\bmod N. \tag{17}
\]
Equations (13), (14), and (17) involve only bounded integer arithmetic.

Evaluating them for \(a=2,\ldots,29401\), in the six consecutive blocks
\[
[2,5001],\ [5002,10001],\ [10002,15001],\ [15002,20001],\ [20002,25001],\ [25002,29401],
\]
gives 150 values satisfying (13). The least resulting value of \(F(a)\) is
\[
F(25127)=16636127. \tag{18}
\]
For illustration, the arithmetic at this minimizing entry is
\[
2^{25127}\bmod N=144540,
\qquad b_{25127}=144540-25127=119413,
\]
\[
119413\equiv13573\equiv49\pmod{196},
\]
\[
\delta_{25127}=119413-13573=105840=196\cdot540,
\]
\[
t_{25127}=(540\cdot131)\bmod2807=565,
\]
and hence
\[
F(25127)=25127+29400\cdot565=16636127.
\]
The next two smallest outputs are \(16956927\) (from \(a=22527\)) and \(17037127\) (from \(a=14527\)); all the remaining outputs are larger. The finite scan’s mathematical role is precisely to establish
\[
F(a)\ge16636127
\]
whenever (13) holds. Since
\[
16636127>16331503=M,
\]
equation (16) proves that no \(k\) in (10) hits \(13573\). Thus the first \(M\) values do not cover all residues modulo \(N\).

It follows that no complete-coverage cutoff can be at most \(M\). Indeed, if coverage were complete at some \(m\le M\), it would remain complete after enlarging the range to \(1\le k\le M\), contrary to the missing residue just proved. Therefore
\[
a(550172)\ge M+1=16331504. \tag{19}
\]

## 4. The relevant prime index

It remains to identify the prime occurring in the conjectured bound. A finite sieve of Eratosthenes up to \(8165753\) gives
\[
\pi(8165753)=550172. \tag{20}
\]
For completeness, this calculation is obtained by starting with the integers \(2,3,\ldots,8165753\), and, successively for every unmarked integer \(p\le\sqrt{8165753}<2858\), marking the multiples \(p^2,p^2+p,\ldots\). Every composite number in the interval is marked, because it has a prime divisor at most its square root, and no prime is marked. Counting the unmarked entries gives 550172. The last unmarked entry is \(8165753\); equivalently, the same sieve gives \(\pi(8165752)=550171\). Thus
\[
p_{550172}=8165753. \tag{21}
\]
Only the upper bound \(p_{550172}\le8165753\) is needed for the contradiction, but (20) gives the exact value.

Combining (19) and (21),
\[
a(550172)\ge16331504
   =2(8165753-1)
   =2(p_{550172}-1).
\]
Hence
\[
a(550172)<2(p_{550172}-1)
\]
is false. Therefore the assertion that \(a(n)<2(p_n-1)\) for every positive integer \(n\) is disproved.
